fixes.explanation: The verse says, “Wail, O cypress, for the cedar has fallen…” (Zechariah 11:2). The cedar was the big tree of the forest, and when it goes down, the trees around it are told to cry out. Nobody in that forest is feeling chipper. This is a sad moment for Lebanon, friend.

A song would be nice, friend, but this isn't a time for singing. The verse says the cedar has fallen and the majestic trees are ruined, so the cypress is told to wail (Zechariah 11:2). When a tree like that hits the ground, nobody grabs a microphone. The passage calls for crying out instead.

I wish this one were a nap, baker. The word to the cypress is “Wail, O cypress, for the cedar has fallen…” (Zechariah 11:2). The cedar has fallen and the majestic trees are ruined. That's a call to cry out, so rest isn't what the verse says.

That's right, baker. The cedars aren't alone in this. The cypress is told to wail, and so are the oaks of Bashan, because “…the dense forest has been cut down!” (Zechariah 11:2). The whole forest is caught up in it.

The shepherds are wailing in this verse, friend, and the text doesn't mention any chase. It gives the lions' reason, and the reason is the thickets. It says the young lions roar because “…the thickets of the Jordan are destroyed.” (Zechariah 11:3).

The verse says the opposite, baker. It says, “Even their own shepherds have no compassion on them.” (Zechariah 11:5). The buyers slaughter them without remorse, and their own shepherds have no compassion. It's a heavy verse.

That's it, baker. The LORD says He will “…cause each man to fall into the hands of his neighbor and his king, who will devastate the land…” (Zechariah 11:6). The hands are his neighbor's and his king's. That's who the verse names.
Pharaoh isn't named here, friend. The LORD says each man will fall into the hands of “…his neighbor and his king…” (Zechariah 11:6). Those are the ones the verse names.
The strongest ones aren't who the verse names, friend. The prophet pastures the flock “…especially the afflicted of the flock.” (Zechariah 11:7). Strong or not, the verse points to the afflicted.

I wish that were true, friend, but the text says otherwise. The prophet says, “My soul grew impatient with the flock, and their souls also detested me.” (Zechariah 11:8). He grew impatient with them, and they detested him. This pasture has a lot of tension in it.

Asking for a new flock would be a whole different move, friend, and the text doesn't show it. He speaks to this flock and says, “I will no longer shepherd you.” (Zechariah 11:9). No request, just him stepping away from the job. I think that's a sad thing to hear.

Verse 5 has the sellers talking, baker, but that's not what the prophet does here. He says, “I will no longer shepherd you.” (Zechariah 11:9). He stops being their shepherd, and the text doesn't mention a market.

A deal with some traders would be small next to this, baker. The text says cutting the staff called Favor revokes “…the covenant I had made with all the nations.” (Zechariah 11:10). That's all the nations, not one group of traders. Big staff, big snap.

The text says they did know, friend. It says, “…the afflicted of the flock who were watching me knew that it was the word of the LORD.” (Zechariah 11:11). They were watching, and they knew it was the word of the LORD.

The high priest would make for a fancy delivery, friend, but he isn't who the text names. The LORD says, “Throw it to the potter…” (Zechariah 11:13). The silver goes to the potter, and the high priest never shows up in the verse.

Thirty pieces of silver in hand, and he still doesn't keep it, friend. After the LORD says, “Throw it to the potter…” he writes, “So I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them to the potter in the house of the LORD.” (Zechariah 11:13). He does what the LORD says.

Shearing is regular shepherd work, friend, but that's not the verse. The LORD says this shepherd “…will devour the flesh of the choice sheep…” (Zechariah 11:16). This is a heavy verse, and it isn't about wool.
